en.content: In a reflecting telescope, a secondary mirror is used to:

options.content: make chromatic aberration zero
remove spherical aberration
reduce the problem of mechanical support
move the eyepiece outside the telescopic tube

en.explanation:
Reflecting telescopes, also known as reflectors, use a set of mirrors instead of lenses to gather and focus light. The primary mirror (usually a concave mirror) gathers the incoming light and reflects it to a focus point. The secondary mirror is used to redirect this focused light out to where it can be conveniently observed.

In other words, the secondary mirror in a reflecting telescope is used to move the eyepiece outside the telescopic tube, where the image can be comfortably viewed. This is especially important for large telescopes, where the focus point may be inside the telescope tube and inaccessible without a secondary mirror.

en.content: Certain galvanometers have a fixed core made of non magnetic metallic material. The function of this metallic material is

options.content: to bring the coil to rest quickly
to produce large deflecting torque on the coil
to oscillate the coil in magnetic field for longer period of time
to make the magnetic field radial

en.explanation:
The function of the non-magnetic metallic core in a galvanometer is to provide a path for the induced current generated by the moving coil in the magnetic field. This induced current opposes the motion of the coil and brings it to rest quickly due to the effect known as eddy current damping.

When the coil swings past its equilibrium position, a change in magnetic flux occurs. According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, this change in magnetic flux generates an induced current, known as an eddy current. The eddy current creates its own magnetic field which opposes the original change in flux, causing the coil to quickly come to rest.
